content: The medication Uceris is specifically approved for the induction of remission in patients with active, mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis. The recommended dosage is 9 mg taken orally every morning for up to 8 weeks. Entocort EC is indicated for the treatment of mild-to-moderate active Crohn's disease affecting the ileum and/or ascending colon. For patients aged 8 years or older and weighing more than 25 kg, the recommended dosage is 9 mg orally every morning for up to 8 weeks, followed by 6 mg every morning for an additional 2 weeks. Its safety and efficacy in children under 8 years of age have not been established. Tarpeyo is approved for reducing the loss of kidney function in adults with primary immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) who are at risk of disease progression. The recommended dosage is 16 mg orally once daily for 9 months. When discontinuing, the dose should be reduced to 8 mg daily for the last 2 weeks of therapy. The safety and efficacy of repeated treatment courses have not been established. Eohilia is indicated for the treatment of eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) in patients aged 11 years and older. The recommended dosage is 2 mg (10 mL) orally twice daily for 12 weeks. However, its safety and efficacy for EoE treatment beyond 12 weeks have not been demonstrated. Eohilia has orphan drug designation for slowing the progression of immunoglobulin A nephropathy and delaying the onset of kidney failure in affected patients. It also has orphan designation for the treatment of primary biliary cholangitis. Budesonide interacts with various medications and substances, primarily through its metabolism by the hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin) or inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine, St. John’s Wort) can significantly alter budesonide levels, leading to increased risk of corticosteroid excess or reduced therapeutic efficacy. In such cases, alternative drugs should be considered, or close monitoring is required. Budesonide also interacts with live vaccines, reducing their efficacy and increasing the risk of infection due to its immunosuppressive effects. Live vaccines such as measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, yellow fever, and rotavirus are contraindicated during budesonide therapy. Additionally, inactivated vaccines (e.g., influenza, hepatitis A/B, pneumococcal) may have reduced effectiveness when administered concurrently with budesonide. Certain medications, such as aluminum hydroxide, magnesium carbonate, and calcium carbonate, can increase gastric pH, potentially causing premature dissolution of extended-release budesonide tablets. This may affect the drug's release properties and absorption in the duodenum. Therapy adjustments and close monitoring are recommended in such cases. Budesonide may also interact with anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin, antithrombin agents), potentially decreasing their effects by increasing blood coagulability or impairing vascular integrity, which could increase bleeding risk. Close monitoring of INR levels is advised. When co-administered with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as aspirin, celecoxib, or ibuprofen, there is an increased risk of gastrointestinal ulceration due to pharmacodynamic synergy. Caution and monitoring are recommended.
